title_original: Jonathas de Andrade wins the 2026 Eye Art & Film Prize
excerpt_original: The Brazilian artist and filmmaker Jonathas de Andrade is the twelfth winner of the Eye Art & Film Prize. De Andrade receives the prize […] Cet article Jonathas de Andrade wins the 2026 Eye Art & Film Prize est apparu en premier sur The Eye of Photography Magazine .

blocks.text: The Brazilian artist and filmmaker Jonathas de Andrade is the twelfth winner of the Eye Art & Film Prize. De Andrade receives the prize for his contribution to the art of the moving image. The jury admires both the way his deeply human work is rooted in the communities in the north-east of Brazil and the carefully constructed worlds he creates through his striking use of colour, sound, rhythm and montage.

As announced at Eye on 19 November during Amsterdam Art Week, Jonathas de Andrade (born in 1982 in Brazil) was selected by an international jury. He will receive €30,000 and a presentation of his work at Eye Filmmuseum. The prize enables the winner to develop new work. The prize is supported by Ammodo Art and Goslings Film & Art Fund.

Documentary and fiction, portraiture, performance and social choreography intermingle in De Andrade’s work. His collaborations with local workers, homeless people and other groups in the Brazilian city of Recife never result in straightforward narratives but allow room for ambiguity and different perspectives from within these communities. The people he meets are not simply subjects in his work; they actively shape how it is made and presented. He also creates carefully constructed worlds thanks to a striking use of colour, sound, rhythm and montage.

In the words of the jury: “The jury praises De Andrade’s deeply human and interdisciplinary practice, which moves seamlessly between film, photography, installation, performance and archival research. His work is rooted in Recife, in the north-east of Brazil, and in the history, communities, physical spaces and everyday activities of the city. He is closely connected to the place where his work is set and, at the same time, he addresses wider questions about identity, memory and social history.”

What particularly impresses the jury is his generous approach: “De Andrade’s work emerges from encounters with people, quietly blurring the boundaries between artist and subject, artwork and lived experience.”
